one_liner: Header-only open-addressing hash map/set beating std::unordered_map on memory and, per two independent suites, speed.
what_it_does: Drop-in replacement for std::unordered_map/unordered_set, built on open addressing (a flat probed array) instead of chaining, so it needs far less per-entry overhead (about 1 byte/entry). Header-only, same STL-style interface, plus optional serialize()/unserialize() to dump a whole table to a file or stream. Values must be copyable-and-movable or movable-only; erase()/insert() invalidate iterators and value references more readily than std::unordered_map does.
how_it_is_fast: Uses Google sparsehash's 'sparsetable' layout: slots are grouped (SPP_GROUP_SIZE, 32 or 64) and each group carries a bitmap (group_bm_type in spp.h) marking which slots are occupied, so mostly-empty regions cost almost nothing to store. Open addressing itself avoids std::unordered_map's per-node allocation and pointer chasing. The README says this layout also keeps the resize memory spike small compared to a plain open-addressing table, though the resize algorithm itself wasn't inspected this session. Integer keys get a built-in bit-mixing default hash to avoid the pathological slowdown that sequential/identity-hashed keys cause on non-present lookups.
when_to_use: Memory-constrained C++ workloads (embedded, large in-memory indexes) where per-entry overhead or resize memory spikes from std::unordered_map/dense_hash_map are the bottleneck
Integer or string key/value hash tables in the hundreds-of-thousands to ~100M entry range, matching the benchmarked workload
Projects on pre-C++11 or older MSVC/g++ toolchains that can't take the C++11 requirement of greg7mdp/parallel-hashmap
Throughput-oriented insert/lookup/erase workloads, not strict latency SLAs, with no need for concurrent writers
Need built-in binary serialize()/unserialize() of the whole table to a file or stream
when_not_to_use: Peak throughput matters most: google::dense_hash_map beats sparsepp on insert, lookup, and delete in the author's own bench.md
Any C++11+ toolchain is available: the author's README now recommends greg7mdp/parallel-hashmap (or gtl) instead of sparsepp
Code holds long-lived references or pointers into the map across insert()/erase() — sparsepp invalidates them more aggressively than std::unordered_map
Code uses a sparse_hash_map/set after moving from it — moved-from tables segfault on further use (issue #83, open, unresolved)
Hash quality is uncertain (e.g. an unmixed identity hash on integer keys) — spp degrades badly or times out per Ankerl 2022

integration.min_toolchain: Works with C++03; C++11 features (move semantics, initializer lists) auto-detected and used if the compiler supports them. Tested on VS2010-2015, g++, clang++.
integration.platforms: Windows, Linux, macOS; x86/x64, no SIMD required. Compiler/platform detection macros derived from Boost for portability.
integration.thread_safety: Follows std library container rules: concurrent reads on one table from multiple threads are safe; if one thread writes to a table, all other reads/writes to that same table must be externally synchronized; separate table instances are fully independent (documented in README).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same STL-style interface as std::unordered_map/set, but erase()/insert() invalidate iterators and value references more aggressively, and a moved-from table is left broken (open bug) rather than empty.

gotchas: Moved-from sparse_hash_map/set is left in an inconsistent state; calling find() or other operations on it segfaults (issue #83, open as of 2026-09-23; author's own workaround suggestion is to switch to parallel-hashmap)
insert()/erase() can invalidate references and pointers to stored values, unlike std::unordered_map where references survive unless a rehash occurs
Default integer hash does bit-mixing to dodge sequential-key pathologies; a user-supplied hash with similar low-order bits across keys needs the SPP_MIX_HASH macro or collisions increase
Copy construction/assignment is slow relative to the baseline (per verification caveats)
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick sparsepp over google::dense_hash_map when the final table size is unknown and you can't absorb dense_hash_map's larger resize memory spike; pick it over tsl::robin_map/ska::flat_hash_map/emhash mainly when stuck on a pre-C++11 toolchain, since for any C++11+ project the author's own README recommends parallel-hashmap (not sparsepp) over those newer designs too.
verified_claims_summary: Two independent third-party suites (not the author's own graphs) show spp::sparse_hash_map beating libstdc++'s std::unordered_map: Ankerl 2022 (clang++13, -O3 -march=native, Intel i7-8700) measured geometric-mean speedups of 1.98-2.03x depending on hash choice, with number-find up to 2.51x, but spp timed out on integer insert/erase/find when using an unmixed identity hash. Tessil's 2017 shootout (Clang 5.0 with libstdc++, 200K-3M entries) measured 1.11-3.31x faster successful lookups and 1.15-5.60x faster misses, with inserts ranging 0.61-1.47x (slower than std::unordered_map on string keys).
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-19, BSD-3-Clause, 1311 stars, not a fork or archived) but the author's own README now steers users to greg7mdp/parallel-hashmap for any C++11+ project, calling it a better speed/memory trade-off than sparsepp.
